newsitem.title: USA: Meager IPO returns keep damper on demand.
newsitem.headline: Meager IPO returns keep damper on demand.

text.p: Relatively meagre returns have kept demand in check for initial public offerings and could mean lower prices and buying opportunities for smaller investors.

For companies that went public in 1996, average gains through last week were 14.5 percent, according to Securities Data Co. That compares with gains of 26 percent, 20 percent and 22 percent for the Dow Industrials, the Standard & Poor's 500 Index and the Nasdaq Composite, respectively.

For companies that went public this year, the average gain is 7.45 percent. That compares more favourably with the major averages in 1997, but many IPO buyers and sellers expect a gain of 10 percent as a rule of thumb for a successful IPO.
Those gains come hard-won, however, as investment banks have cut prices after finding weak demand.
Of the 114 IPOs priced so far this year, 20 sold above the range, 37 sold below expectations and the rest sold where expected.
"Usually it's a bell curve with most deals in the middle and an equal number of deals on either side," said Richard Peterson of Securities Data.

The lower prices mean individual investors have a better chance at buying into an initial public offering, but they should examine prospectuses carefully because high quality companies have been scarce, some analysts say.
Securities Data said 29 percent of the companies that went public this year have lost money.
"There's no specific trend right now other than 'Big is in,'" said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket.
Spooked by the poor returns and concerns about the broader stock market, large institutional investors have been shying away from small, high-risk deals.
Instead, they are choosing large deals that offer the safety of stronger financial histories and better liquidity during a possible downturn.
"(Buyers have) been very discerning. They are looking very closely at transactions and are exercising price discipline," said Brian Hehir, co-head of equity markets at Merrill Lynch & Co.

The number of IPOs registered with regulators that have not yet gone public "is pretty low for middle March, though. We should be approaching peak backlog at this point with the end of the quarter coming," he said.
Analysts see no end in sight for the cautious mood, which has meant bargain basement IPO prices, although dollar volume remains strong, analysts said.

"My sense is what we have is people missing the sizzle. We had some quite large deals done very quietly in the first quarter," said Hehir, noting solid gains for Nationwide Financial's $480 million IPO and Trigon's $200 million market debut.

IPO activity was quiet last week, with nine deals raising $362 million, according to MCM CorporateWatch. After a mostly lackluster week, NeoMagic Corp. and Guitar Centre Inc. both posted higher opening premiums of about 20 percent Friday.

NeoMagic, which makes multimedia accelerators for personal computer notebooks, had been expected to perform well based on its low offering price. The deal was initially filed to price at between $7 and $9 but finally sold for $12 a share.
"It did very well, but of course it did at that discount," one underwriter said. "When was the last time you saw a deal come out of Morgan Stanley at $7?"
She said that the low price first set by Morgan Stanley could signal that underwriters have begun to discount IPOs sharply from the very first, which could signal a healthier future market.
Deals that look hot this week include Cell Therapeutics Inc., which develops drugs that use small molecules, and Colonial Downs, according to Fitzgibbon.
